title: How to Price Roofing Jobs: A Step-by-Step Method
description: A step-by-step method for pricing roofing jobs by the square, covering takeoff, waste, labor hours, disposal, permits, overhead and markup or margin.

p: Pricing a roof is mostly a matter of counting the right things in the right units and then pricing each line with your own numbers. This guide walks through the method in the order you would build it in Built2Bid, from measurements to the final price.
The example in this guide uses round numbers for illustration only. Replace every figure with your own supplier quotes, recent invoices, labor rate and local permit fees.

blocks.h: Measure in squares and count each roof plane
p: Roofing is priced by the square, which is 100 square feet of roof surface. Measure each roof plane separately, including garages, porches and dormers, then add the totals. Write each quantity on its own line with its unit so the takeoff matches the estimate.
Count linear items the same way. Eaves and rakes give you drip edge in linear feet, and the ridge gives you ridge cap and ridge vent. Count pipe penetrations as each.

blocks.h: Add waste to materials, not to labor
p: Shingles, underlayment and ridge cap are ordered with extra for cuts, valleys, hips and breakage. Choose a waste allowance based on roof complexity and your own job history, then apply it to material quantities only. Labor is priced on the measured squares, not the ordered squares.
Confirm the waste figure with your supplier, since bundle and roll sizes change what you can order.

blocks.h: Price labor by the square and by the hour
p: Use separate labor lines. Shingle installation labor is priced per square. Flashing and detail work is priced per hour because it varies with the number of penetrations, valleys and transitions. Tear-off is also labor, so set a labor-hours figure for it per square based on your crew's own records.

Labor cost equals labor hours multiplied by your hourly rate. Your rate should cover wages, payroll taxes, insurance, vehicles and tools, not just the hourly wage. Track actual hours on a few jobs and use those figures in future estimates.

blocks.h: Equipment, disposal and decking
p: Tear-off generates debris. Price the dumpster as each and include it in the Tear-Off and Disposal section. If you use a lift, a magnet sweeper or other equipment, add it as an equipment cost type line with its own quantity and unit.

Hidden deck damage cannot be measured until the old roofing is off. Price replacement decking per sheet so the customer sees a clear unit price for each sheet that needs replacing. Agree on how extra sheets will be approved before you start that work.

blocks.h: Permits and pass-through charges
p: Building permit fees are set by the local building department, and requirements vary by location. Ask the department whether a roof permit is required, what it costs and which inspections apply to your job.

You can show the permit as a pass-through charge at cost, so it appears on the proposal without markup. Confirm with a tax professional how sales tax applies to permit fees and materials in your area, and ask an attorney to review how pass-through charges are written in your contract.

blocks.h: Overhead and the markup or margin decision
p: Add overhead as a percentage of direct cost, based on your own annual overhead divided by your annual direct costs. Then choose how to price the job. Built2Bid can price an estimate with either markup on cost or target gross margin, and it shows the other number for reference.
Markup and margin are different. Markup is added to cost, so Price = Cost × (1 + Markup). Margin is a share of the final price, so Price = Cost ÷ (1 − Margin). Check both before you choose one.

blocks.h: Simplified example
p: This simplified example covers only the tear-off, shingle, dumpster and building permit lines. A real estimate includes every section above, including decking, flashing, ventilation, cleanup and any equipment.
All figures below are for illustration only. Replace them with your own quotes, hours and rates.
formula: Example: 20 squares × 1.10 = 22 squares of shingles (illustration only, 10 percent waste)
Example: 20 squares × 1 labor hour per square = 20 labor hours (illustration only)
Example: 20 labor hours × $50 per hour = $1,000 tear-off and shingle labor
Example: 22 squares × $100 per square = $2,200 shingle material
Example: 1 dumpster × $400 = $400 disposal
Example: $3,600 × 0.10 = $360 overhead
Example: $3,600 + $360 = $3,960 total cost
Example: $3,960 × 1.25 = $4,950 price with 25% markup
Example: $3,960 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $4,950 price with 20% margin
Example: 1 building permit × $200 = $200 passed through at cost
Example: $4,950 + $200 = $5,150 total on the proposal for these lines

blocks.h: Quality tips and code items inspectors check
p: Local editions and amendments of the International Residential Code vary, so confirm requirements with your local building department and ask which inspections apply to your job. Follow manufacturer installation instructions for every product. These tips show where each code topic should change what you include in the estimate.
list: R905 (Requirements for roof coverings) covers underlayment, fastening and installation by material, which an inspector may look at. Include the underlayment, ice and water shield, nails and labor that your chosen installation method calls for.

R908 (Reroofing) covers recovering versus replacing and reinstalling flashing. Decide whether the job is a tear-off or a recover before you price it. A second layer adds tear-off labor and disposal, so price those lines separately and confirm with the building department whether recovering is allowed.

R903 (Weather protection) covers roof flashing and drainage. Include drip edge, step and counter flashing by the linear foot, and allow flashing and detail work hours for valleys, walls and penetrations.

R806 (Roof ventilation) covers roof ventilation. Price ridge vent by the linear foot and pipe boots as each. If the design combines ridge vents with a powered attic fan, check the manufacturer warranty before you quote and state the arrangement in the proposal.

R803 (Roof sheathing) covers roof sheathing, and R802 (Wood roof framing) covers wood roof framing. Price replacement decking per sheet. If framing repairs are found, price them as a separate line with labor hours, and ask the building department what review applies before that work starts.

blocks.h: What is changing for roofing contractors and how to reflect it in a bid
p: Some roofing products face long order backlogs, and specialty items and large orders can be hit hardest. Confirm delivery with your supplier before you quote a start date, and set a price validity date on the proposal so a long wait does not leave you holding a price that no longer covers the materials.

Storm work is getting harder to get paid for. State regulators are looking at how insurers handle roof claims, and some contractors are moving away from contracts that depend on insurance money. If you take storm work, have an attorney review your contract terms and state clearly in the proposal who is responsible for payment.

Insurance settlement terms are tightening, with higher deductibles, more actual-cash-value payouts and stricter matching rules. That makes documentation more important. Keep dated photos, measurements, a line-item estimate and a signed scope so you can show what the claim covers. How these changes apply varies by state and insurer, so check locally.

Ventilation is also drawing attention. Under R806 (Roof ventilation), attic ventilation is the topic to check, and combining ridge vents with powered attic fans is flagged as a likely warranty problem. Check manufacturer instructions and warranty terms, and confirm with the building department how the design will be reviewed in your area.

blocks.h: Putting it together
p: Work the method in order: measure squares and linear items, add waste to materials, price labor by the square and by the hour, add equipment and disposal, pass permits through at cost, then add overhead and choose markup or margin. Check each line against your own supplier quotes and recent invoices before you send anything.

In Built2Bid, you can organise the estimate into the sections above, with line items for quantity, unit, unit cost and cost type. Per-section settings let you choose whether the customer sees item names, prices or totals only, which keeps the proposal easy to read at a glance. Sales tax applies only to lines marked taxable, and adjustments and discounts apply before tax.
Licensing and contract terms vary, so check requirements with your state licensing board, a tax professional or an attorney.

title: How to Price Siding Jobs: A Step-by-Step Method
description: Step-by-step method for pricing siding jobs: takeoff in squares, materials with waste, labor hours, disposal, permits, overhead, and markup or margin.

p: Siding bids are mostly arithmetic done in the right units. Measure in squares for panels, linear feet for trim and fascia, and rolls for house wrap, then price each line with your own costs and your own labor rate.

This guide follows the order most estimates are built: takeoff, materials with waste, labor, removal and disposal, permits, overhead, and then markup or margin. Use your own supplier quotes and recent invoices throughout.

blocks.h: Measure and take off quantities
p: Start with a takeoff of each elevation being sided. Measure wall area and convert it to squares, where one square is 100 square feet. Subtract large openings such as windows and doors, but keep the trim and flashing they require as their own lines.
Measure perimeters for corners, starter strip, soffit and fascia. Count outside corners, J-channel and openings separately.

Built2Bid's area and perimeter calculators can do the arithmetic. Each estimate is organised in sections with line items showing quantity, unit, unit cost and cost type (material, labor, equipment, subcontractor or other). Keep the units the same as your supplier's: squares for panels, pieces for J-channel and outside corners, rolls for house wrap, square feet for soffit, linear feet for fascia wrap, and boxes for fasteners.

blocks.h: Price materials with waste
p: Order from the takeoff plus a waste allowance that reflects the cuts on your job, such as gables, dormers and small wall sections. Check the waste percentage against your own past jobs and your supplier's guidance.
Price each material line from a current supplier quote, not from memory. Quotes can change, so note the date and the validity period.
list: House wrap (roll) for the wall area, including the overlaps your crew uses.
Siding panels (square) for the net area plus waste.
J-channel and outside corners (piece) counted from openings and corners.
Soffit (square foot) and fascia wrap (linear foot) from eave and rake measurements.
Fasteners (box) counted from the squares, using the quantity your manufacturer's instructions call for.

blocks.h: Estimate labor hours and labor rate
p: Labor is hours multiplied by your fully loaded labor rate. Build hours per square and per linear foot of trim from your own job history, and adjust for tear-off, height, number of stories and the number of openings.
Price siding installation per square, trim and soffit installation per linear foot, and cleanup as a lump sum.

Group trim in its own section of the estimate, so the trim and soffit hours are easy to see and check. Whether trim and soffit take the most labor on your jobs is a judgment to test against your own job history, not something to assume.

blocks.h: Removal, disposal and equipment
p: Price tear-off of existing siding per square. Count disposal as each load or unit you will haul, using your own disposal cost.

Add equipment such as ladders, scaffolding, lifts or a dumpster as separate equipment lines, using rental quotes or your own equipment cost. Partial repairs often need protection of landscaping and access planning, so include those hours too.

blocks.h: Permits, licensing and inspection time
p: Requirements vary. Contact the local building department about permit fees, whether a permit applies to your scope, and which inspections apply to siding work. Contact the state licensing board for contractor licensing rules, and a tax professional about sales tax on materials.
Add the permit fee, and the time to schedule and meet the inspector, as their own lines so they are not hidden in labor.

blocks.h: Overhead and contingency
p: Overhead covers the costs of running the business that do not appear on a single job, such as insurance, vehicles, tools, office costs and unbilled time. Spread your overhead across billable hours, or add a percentage to direct cost based on your own records.
Add a contingency line for known unknowns, such as rot under old siding. State in the proposal what is excluded so the contingency is not used to cover gaps in scope.

blocks.h: Markup or target margin
p: Built2Bid prices each estimate with either markup on cost or target gross margin, and shows the other figure for reference. Price = Cost × (1 + Markup). Price = Cost ÷ (1 − Margin). A 25 percent markup on cost gives a 20 percent gross margin, so pick one method, then check the other number before you send the bid.
Sales tax applies only to lines marked taxable, and adjustments or discounts apply before tax. Confirm with a tax professional how tax applies to your materials and labor in your state.

blocks.h: Simplified example
p: This simplified example covers only the siding panel and siding installation lines, plus markup, for 10 squares of wall. A real estimate includes every section above, including removal, house wrap, trim, flashing, disposal, permits and overhead. The numbers are for illustration only and are not prices to use.
formula: Example: 10 squares × 1.10 (10% waste) = 11 squares of siding panels
Example: 11 squares × $200 = $2,200 for siding panels
Example: 10 squares × 3 labor hours per square = 30 labor hours
Example: 30 hours × $60 per hour = $1,800 for siding installation
Example: $4,000 × (1 + 0.25) = $5,000 price at 25% markup
Example: $4,000 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $5,000 price at 20% target margin

blocks.h: Quality tips and code items inspectors check
p: These items affect what you include in the estimate. Local editions and amendments vary, so confirm each item with the local building department, and follow the manufacturer's installation instructions for every product.
list: R703 (Exterior covering) covers siding, the water-resistive barrier and flashing. An inspector may look at how these are installed. Include the house wrap, its fasteners and the labor to install the barrier ahead of the siding.

R703.4 (Flashing) covers flashing around windows, doors and wall penetrations. An inspector may look at these details. Count every opening and penetration in the takeoff, and price flashing material and labor for each one instead of leaving it to the trim section.

R703.8 (Anchored stone and masonry veneer) covers anchored veneer. If the job includes anchored veneer, price the anchoring work and its labor, and ask the building department whether it falls within your scope.

R316 (Foam plastic) covers foam plastic. If foam sheathing, foam trim or other foam accessories are part of the job, add the material and the labor to fit them, and ask the building department how the inspector will review them.

Fiber cement attachment requirements have changed across editions of the residential code. Confirm which edition and amendments apply, and price the fasteners and labor for the attachment method the building department accepts.

blocks.h: What is changing for siding contractors and how to reflect it in a bid
p: Vinyl is usually the easiest product to schedule, because material is almost always in stock locally. Specialty lines and colors can stretch the calendar. Disruptions in resin, steel and fiber cement production have also stretched lead times for many cladding types. Check local stock and lead time for each product before you commit to a start date.

In the bid, confirm lead times with the supplier in writing, price from a current quote, and set a price validity date on the proposal so a delayed order does not quietly change the price. For specialty products, state in the terms what happens if material arrives late.

Fiber cement attachment rules can differ by local edition, and high-wind coastal sites can fall outside what the prescriptive tables reflect. Ask the building department early how attachment is to be handled at your site, and budget time for that review.

Partial siding repairs after storm damage can turn into scope disputes. Whether a claim covers matching depends on the policy wording and the facts of the loss. Document the damage with photos, put the scope in writing, and talk with an attorney or the homeowner's insurer before agreeing to match a full elevation.

blocks.h: Putting it together
p: Work in the order above: takeoff in squares, linear feet, rolls and boxes; materials with waste from current quotes; labor hours at your rate, with trim in its own section; then removal, disposal, equipment, permits, overhead and contingency; and finally markup or margin.

Check each line against your own invoices and review the totals before you send the proposal. Requirements vary for permits, licensing, tax and contract terms, so confirm those with the local building department, the state licensing board, a tax professional or an attorney.

title: How to Calculate Your Labor Rate as a Contractor
description: Learn how to build a billable hourly labor rate from wage, labor burden and non-billable time, with a worked example for residential contractors.

p: Your labor rate is the number that turns hours into a price. If you charge the same hourly figure you pay a worker, the work is underpriced before you have covered the costs that sit around that worker.

This guide shows how to build a billable hourly labor rate from the wage you pay, the labor burden on top of it and the time you cannot bill. It uses one simplified example, and you should replace every figure with your own costs.

blocks.h: Why the rate you pay is not the rate you charge
p: The wage on a pay stub is only part of what it costs to have a crew member on a job. Payroll taxes, insurance, benefits and paid time off are added on top. There are also paid hours that produce nothing you can invoice, such as travel to supply houses, callbacks, shop time and waiting for an inspection to be scheduled.
Your billing rate has to recover all of that and still leave a profit. If you charge only the wage, you pay for the non-billable hours out of your margin.

blocks.h: Start with the wage you actually pay
p: Begin with the hourly wage you pay each worker in the role you are pricing. If you are a sole operator, use the pay you take from the business as your wage, not zero.
Use your own payroll records and recent pay stubs as the source. Do not copy a wage from another contractor or from a general table.

blocks.h: Add labor burden to the wage
p: Labor burden is the extra cost of employing someone beyond their wage. Your tax professional can confirm which payroll taxes apply in your state and how to treat each item, since requirements vary. Gather these items from your own records and invoices:
list: Employer payroll taxes that apply to wages
Workers' compensation and any other insurance tied to payroll
Health, retirement or other benefits you contribute to
Paid holidays, vacation and sick time, which are paid but not worked
Required licensing or certification costs for the crew, if you carry them as labor costs
formula: Burdened cost per paid hour = Wage × (1 + Burden rate)
Burden rate = Annual burden costs ÷ Annual wages

blocks.h: Count the hours you can bill
p: Paid hours are not the same as billable hours. A worker paid for 40 hours in a week may spend several of those hours on work you cannot invoice. Check your records over a full period, not one good week.

IRC Section R105, Permits, covers which work needs a permit. Chapter 1 is often amended locally, so ask your building department which work needs a permit and which inspections may apply, since local editions and amendments vary. Time spent on that paperwork is non-billable and belongs in your count. Common non-billable time in residential trades includes:
list: Travel between shops, supply houses and job sites
Estimating, site visits and proposal work
Callbacks and warranty fixes you do not charge for
Permit applications, inspection scheduling and paperwork
Training, toolbox meetings and vehicle or tool maintenance
Waiting on other trades, materials or inspections
formula: Non-billable share = Non-billable hours ÷ Paid hours
Billable hours = Paid hours − Non-billable hours

blocks.h: Calculate the cost per billable hour
p: Spread the full cost of each paid hour across the hours you can actually bill. The result is the cost you need to recover for every billable hour.
Use your own annual figures where you have them, taken from payroll records, invoices and time logs.
formula: Cost per billable hour = Burdened cost per paid hour ÷ (1 − Non-billable share)

blocks.h: Add margin or markup to reach your billing rate
p: The cost per billable hour is what the labor costs you. It is not yet a profitable rate. Choose a target gross margin or a markup and apply it to that cost. The same price can be written either way.

A 25 percent markup on cost and a 20 percent gross margin produce the same price, because they describe the same relationship in different ways. Use one method consistently so your bids can be compared.
formula: Price = Cost × (1 + Markup)
Price = Cost ÷ (1 − Margin)

blocks.h: Simplified example: labor rate for one worker
p: This simplified example covers only the wage, burden, billable hours and billing rate lines below. A real estimate includes every section above. All figures are for illustration only and are not a benchmark for your area or trade.
Recalculate with your own figures. The example rate applies to one worker under these assumptions only.
formula: Example: $30 × (1 + 0.20) = $36 burdened cost per paid hour
Example: 2,000 paid hours × $36 = $72,000 burdened labor cost per year
Example: 2,000 paid hours × 25% = 500 non-billable hours
Example: 2,000 − 500 = 1,500 billable hours
Example: $72,000 ÷ 1,500 billable hours = $48 cost per billable hour
Example: $48 × (1 + 0.25) = $60 billing rate with a 25% markup
Example: $48 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $60 billing rate with a 20% margin

blocks.h: What is changing for contractors and how to reflect it in a bid
p: Several cost pressures are affecting how small contractors price work. Check how each one applies in your area and your trade before changing your numbers.

Lead times for some long-lead materials, such as structural steel and custom components, are being built into schedules more often. Order earlier where needed, tie purchase timing to the bid, and confirm lead times with suppliers before you commit to a start date.

Insurance is becoming a larger cost line for many small contractors, and some absorb premium increases rather than pricing them in. Build expected increases into the burden in your labor rate and into the overhead recovery in each bid, and review the figures with your insurance agent.

Material prices are moving unevenly by category. For jobs that start well after the estimate date, some contractors add escalation clauses to the bid. Set a price validity date on each proposal, and ask an attorney whether an escalation clause fits your contracts and your state.

blocks.h: Use your own numbers
p: For licensing requirements and contract terms, confirm with your state licensing board, a tax professional or an attorney, because requirements vary. Keep a record of each figure and where it came from so you can show the basis for your bids.
list: Wages and burden from payroll records and tax filings
Insurance costs from your current policy and renewal notices
Billable hours from a time log kept for at least one full period
Permit fees from the local building department
Supplier quotes and recent invoices for materials and subcontracted work

blocks.h: Putting it together
p: Start with the wage you pay, add labor burden, remove non-billable time from the paid hours, and divide the cost by the billable hours that remain. Then apply a markup or margin to reach the rate you charge. Recalculate when wages, insurance or your non-billable share change.

In Built2Bid, labor can be entered as line items with a cost type of labor, alongside materials, equipment, subcontractor and other costs. The quantity calculators can help estimate labor hours, and each section can control what the customer sees on the proposal. Follow manufacturer installation instructions for any product you price.
